Note.Content: The exact referent of אַגֻדָּה here has been under discussion. According to Shalom Paul, it refers to "the tightly fitted vault of heaven otherwise called רָקִיעַ or חוּג." Andersen and Freedman analyse the meaning of the word at length, and suggest the translation "its structures", considering the suffix as referring to מַעַלֹותֹו . The image would be of God's sanctuary with one part in heaven and the other on earth. Semantically, the question is whether אַגֻדָּה means a foundation of a building or its upper part.

MT-K יבּחר has been variously read (יְבֻחַר pual | יִבָּחֶר niphal) | MT-Q יְחֻבַּר from חבר "to join". Most English versions follow MT-Q (RSV NRSV "is joined with" | NJPS "is reckoned among" | NIV "is among" | REB "is counted among") as also most commentaries. Seouw takes the MT-K as qal, and reads the phrase as interrogative (rhetorical question) "Who is the one who chooses?". Murphy also takes it as interrogative, "who can be set apart?" (understanding בחר here as "to be set apart"). The existence of a pual form has been questioned (cf. Seouw, and Gordis, The Book of Job, 418, on JOB 36:21).

Here בלל could have a negative connotation, as in GEN 11:7,9. See the note in MacIntosh, who translates it as "vitiated", a meaning that would "fit this particular context and the reference to the spoiled cake better than the other sense of the verb, viz. ‘mix’, ‘mingle’, though the two senses are clearly related". HALOT suggests the meaning "to be thrown about", without explanation (the reference to Rudolph, which does not appear in HALAT, is misleading).
For a discussion, see the note in Tate.

Note.Content: The phrase כְּגֹוב גֹּבָי "like a locust of locusts" is normally taken as a case of dittography from an original כְּגֹבָי "like locusts", as per LXX. Most versions translate it as a collective noun phrase: RSV "like clouds of locusts", NJPS "like piles of hoppers", NJB "like swarms of hoppers", NIV "like swarms of locusts". The Vulgate follows the MT more closely "quasi lucustae lucustarum", "like (the) locusts of locusts".

Most versions and scholars interpret נִּדְגָּלֹות as deriving from דֶגֶל "banner". Another possibility takes דגל as meaning "look' (HALOT | DCH) and the pt. pass. as "sight"; the arguments are well presented by Gerleman, Ruth/Hohelied, p. 182-83 (cf. also Zakovitch, Das Hohelied, p.232-33). If נִּדְגָּלֹות is taken as pointing to the stars (REB CEV), than the meaning here would be "majestic as the stars". In this case, the lexical domain would be "Universe > Intense", and the contextual domain "Beauty | Nature > Human".

Note.Content: The exact meaning of דגר here is much discussed. There is a succession of 3 verbs indicating actions of a mother-bird in relation to eggs. NRSV translates בקע as "hatch" and דגר as "brood", and NJPS the other way round, though interpreting them as practically synonyms | RSV REB "gather", implying a movement that either comes before the hatching or (in some way) after it, as the order in the text suggests. The best course could be to follow the meaning of דגר in JER 17:11, which with more probability points to "hatch".

Note.Content: The way this word is used in this passage shows that the head of the bird is severed at the front but left attached to the rump at the back.

The reason why מוּל is preceded by מִן in this passage is not exactly clear | in view of the context the most plausible explanation is that Balak wants to stress the closeness of Israel | {A:NJB} and {A:REB} have brought this out clearly by using the expression "at my very door".

{A:HOTTP}-B {A:NIV} {A:NJPS} {A:CEV} מֹול | {A:MT} לְמֹואל | {A:RSV} {A:NJB} {A:NRSV} {A:REB} {A:GNT} {L:"left"<SDBH:שְׂמֹאל>} | the interpretation of {A:HOTTP}-B has probably been inspired by the gloss "opposite", which several English translations use to render the word מוּל | though "opposite" can be used to indicate the relative closeness of two locations (e.g. ), it should not be used to indicate opposite directions, which is outside of the scope of the meaning of this word | for that reason the interpretation of {A:RSV} et al. is to be preferred.
It is assumed, along with {A:HOTTP}-B that the אֶדֶר represents a piece of clothing that is worn over the שַׂלְמָה | see for instance TOB "... dessus la tunique, vous enlevez le manteau ..."

Note.Content: Most commentators have argued that the verb should be read as a piel instead of a niphal

Although the passive of σῴζω in the LXX implies the reading of a niph (יִמָּלֵט) cf. Tg) rather than the piel, the verb may not require revocalisation. There may be an implied indefinite object, and the Peshitta does include an object in its translation (see piel Versions, Peshitta).

The passive of διασῴζω in the LXX implies the reading of the niphal (יִמָּלֵט) cf. Vg, Tg, Pesh), but this may be a characteristic alteration by the Versions to assist the sense. The piel, if retained, would have to be interpreted as intransitive, or to share the same object נפשׁו with the verb in the next line.

LEXSense.DefinitionShort: literally: Queen of Heaven; hence: = epithet of a female deity, possibly to be identified with Ishtar or {L:Ashtoreth<SDBH:עַשְׁתֹּרֶת>}; ► worshipped by the Israelites
LEXSense.Comments: The "Queen of Heaven" in Jeremiah is the mother godess. cf. versiones: LXX, Vg, Aq, Sym, Th. A likely identification of the title with the West Semitic Ashtoreth or the Mesopotamian Ishtar is based on the cakes offered to the deity in Jer 7:18; 44:19 which may have been star-shaped. Both Ashtoreth and Ishtar are fertility goddesses identified with Venus, the morning and evening star. Both were offered cakes as part of their cult, though it is only Ishtar in whose image cakes were baked and whose cult held a particular appeal for women. Ishtar was known as the queen or lady of heaven. Queen of Heaven in Jeremiah is therefore a syncretistic deity, combining aspects of Ashtoreth and Ishtar.

LEXSense.Comments: In the post-exilic period an ideology of “bicephalic leadership” seems to have existed, argued on the basis of Zec 6.12-14; 4.2-3,11-14; 8.9-17, Hag 1.12-14.This king-priest duality is found strongly in Chronicles too, which evaluates Israelite history in these very terms of shared leadership. However, neither Jubilees nor Qumran cite Haggai or Zechariah in this context. For further reading cf. SAHD article.

LEXSense.DefinitionShort: = a manifestation of God, often described as a substance that can be poured out, ► through whom the universe is created and animated; it can manifest itself as an invisible force equipping humans with wisdom, skill, and strength for specific tasks; it can also manifest itself as a movement of air through the bodies of animate creatures (breath) or through nature (wind)
= an invisible being associated with God and carrying out his commands, often by taking possession of people and influencing their actions
= inner person of a human or celestial being, associated with emotions, such as joy, grief, worry, courage, anger, willingness, jealousy, etc., but also with inner qualities such as wisdom

= a natural movement of air, blowing in a particular direction, ranging in intensity from a light breeze ({S:01804100800000}) to a heavy blast ({S:01800101900000}); ≈ often regarded as the breath of God, but also associated with things that are without substance and cannot be grasped
literally: (God's) breath; hence: = process by which humans are punished by God, ◄ described as a flaming breath coming from his mouth
literally: breath or wind; hence: = state in which an event does not last, but is over before one knows it
literally: breath or wind; hence: = action by which humans speak words with no substance or value
literally: wind; = a reference to one of the four quarters of heaven, ◄ associated with the wind ► used for orientation purposes
literally: the breath of (one's) mouth; hence: = action by which humans utter words ◄ which are articulated with the help of the breath which leaves the body through the mouth

= the air that is taken in and expelled through the lungs by humans and animals, which makes them live, and which distinguishes them from inanimate objects like idols; ≈ regarded as coming from God; sometimes God is depicted as a breathing being as well
= an amount of space between two objects
literally: space; hence: = process by which humans find relief after a period of hardship

LEXSense.DefinitionShort: literally: moist, watered; hence: = state in which a container is fully filled with liquid to the extent that some of it spills over the rim; ≈ used to denote a state of well-being

literally: to be high; hence: = state in which something perplexes the mind and requires wisdom in order to be dealt with
literally: raised hand; hence: = state in which humans act with confidence
= state in which a certain type of behavior is highly appreciated

literally: to be, become high; hence: = process by which humans or deities acquire an elevated status, either in their own eyes or in the eyes of other people, ≈ which can either be good or bad, depending on whether this status is justified

literally: to make oneself high; hence: = action by which humans or deities bring themselves an elevated status, either in their own eyes or in the eyes of other people, ≈ which can either be good or bad, depending on whether this status is justified

literally: to lift up; hence: = action by which humans pick up (part of) an object with their hands
literally: to lift up; hence: = causative action by which humans restore a building in its previous condition
literally: to lift up; hence: = causative process by which humans are forced to stop engaging in an activity

literally: lifted up voice; hence: = action by which humans speak more loudly than usual
literally: to lift up (one's) voice; hence: = action by which humans speak more loudly than usual
= causative process by which humans take care of young humans while they undergo the natural development of increasing in size and changing physically on their way to being fully grown
= action by which humans raise their hands

literally: to lift up (one's) head; hence: = process by which humans find new confidence

literally: uplifted arm; hence: = action by which humans threaten others with violence
literally: to raise oneself up; hence: = action by which humans refuse to accept someone else's authority
literally: to lift up (one's) hand; hence: = action by which humans refuse to accept someone else's authority
literally: to raise (one's) hand; hence: = action by which humans or celestial beings make a solemn promise

LEXSense.DefinitionShort: meanung unsure, possibly: = action by which humans make an effort to regain control of their body after having been under the influence of an intoxicating substance like wine
meaning unsure, possibly: = action by which humans speak or call out loudly

= information that is known by humans or deities but kept hidden from others
= process by which humans lose flesh or fat on their body; ≈ used figuratively to denote how a nation loses its wealth and prosperity

= state in which humans feel affection for others

= relatively small type of vulture with a long, untidy, light orange-brown feathers on its neck and head, a bare yellow face, and a yellow beak that is longer and less hooked than most vultures; the rest of the body and wings are white with black wing tips; it feeds on the scraps of carrion dropped by larger vultures, since its beak is not strong enough to tear skin and meat easily; usually scavenges scraps on beaches or rubbish dumps and eats the eggs of ground-nesting waterside birds such as plovers, sandpipers, curlews, and others, which it breaks by knocking them with a large stone; ◄ Neophron percnopterus; ► unclean and therefore not to be eaten
literally: one or two wombs; hence: = female persons; ≈ probably a less respectful reference to female slaves or concubines as people you can have sex with and who may bear children for you

= state/process by which humans shake or tremble violently and involuntarily, ◄ caused by fear
meaning unsure; possibly: = state in which the human body is as healthy as that of a young child

= a liquid substance
